disclaimer: Training-simulation help cards for fictional crew. They summarize published measurement methods and are not medical advice or a clinical protocol.

guides.title: Heart rate
guides.what: Beats per minute (bpm) from the assigned wearable, or a manual pulse count.
guides.why: Heart rate follows activity, stress and recovery. A resting value is only comparable with other resting values.
how: For a resting reading, sit quietly for about five minutes before recording.
For a manual count, press two fingers on the wrist or side of the neck and count beats for 30 seconds, then double it.
Record whether the reading was taken at rest, during exercise or during recovery.
guides.context_note: Exercise versus rest: keep the activity context with each reading. Do not compare a reading taken during or right after exercise with a resting baseline.
guides.procedure_label: Ground-based method: the cited pulse procedure was written for use on Earth, not validated in spaceflight.

sources.title: Pulse
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, U.S. National Library of Medicine

guides.title: Blood pressure
guides.what: Systolic and diastolic pressure in mmHg, recorded as a pair.
guides.why: Pressure readings shift with posture, recent activity and cuff fit, so the setup decides whether readings can be compared.
how: Avoid caffeine, exercise and smoking for 30 minutes before measuring.
Sit with the back supported and feet flat, and rest quietly for five minutes.
Wrap a correctly sized cuff on the bare upper arm, with the arm supported at heart level.
Stay still and silent during the reading. Take two readings about one minute apart and record both.
guides.context_note: Cuff setup: use an automatic upper-arm cuff of the correct size. Wrist and finger monitors are not recommended because they give less reliable readings.
guides.procedure_label: Ground-based method: home and clinic cuff procedures assume Earth gravity and a seated posture.

sources.title: Measurement of Blood Pressure in Humans: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association

guides.title: Blood glucose
guides.what: Glucose concentration in mg/dL, with the measurement method and meal context.
guides.why: Glucose changes with meals and with the sampling method, so a value without both is hard to interpret.
how: Wash and dry hands before a fingerstick.
Apply the capillary blood drop to the meter strip and read the result.
Record the method (meter or lab) and the meal context, for example fasting, before a meal or two hours after a meal.
guides.context_note: Glucose meter versus lab method: a self-test meter reads capillary blood and is allowed a wider error than a laboratory plasma glucose method. Record the method with each value and do not mix them in one trend.
guides.procedure_label: Ground-based method: laboratory plasma glucose and meter accuracy limits are defined for ground laboratories and devices.

sources.title: ISO 15197:2013 In vitro diagnostic test systems — Requirements for blood-glucose monitoring systems for self-testing in managing diabetes mellitus
6. Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025

guides.title: Body temperature
guides.what: Body temperature in °C, with the measurement method and the body site.
guides.why: Normal temperature differs by site and time of day, so readings are comparable only when the site matches.
how: Choose one site, such as oral, ear, forehead or armpit, and keep using it.
For an oral reading, wait about 30 minutes after eating, drinking or exercise.
Record the method and site with the value.
guides.context_note: Measurement site: oral, ear, forehead and armpit readings differ. An armpit reading usually runs lower than an oral one, so record the site and compare only like with like.
guides.procedure_label: Ground-based method: normal ranges are published for people on Earth.

sources.title: Body temperature norms
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia, U.S. National Library of Medicine

guides.title: Sleep
guides.what: Sleep as a duration in minutes, or as start and end mission times for one sleep period.
guides.why: Sleep timing and length shape alertness on the next shift. A diary keeps each period separate.
how: After waking, record either the total sleep in minutes or the start and end mission times.
Record the main sleep period and each nap as separate entries.
Do not fill in a missing night from memory days later. Leave it missing.
guides.context_note: Sleep periods: log each sleep period on its own, with either a duration or a start and end time, not both. The adult reference of at least seven hours is a ground-based recommendation, not a mission rule.
guides.procedure_label: Ground-based method: the sleep diary and the sleep-duration consensus come from ground studies.

sources.title: The Consensus Sleep Diary: Standardizing Prospective Sleep Self-Monitoring
Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society

guides.title: Mood self-report
guides.what: A self-rated mood score from 1 to 5 on the project scale mood-1-to-5-v1.
guides.why: A short, repeatable self-rating shows changes over the mission when it is recorded the same way each time.
how: Pick the number from 1 to 5 that best matches how you feel right now.
Rate at a similar point in each day, for example after waking.
Skip a rating rather than guessing it later.
guides.context_note: Self-report: this is a project-defined scale for the simulation, not a validated or clinical assessment. It is never turned into a mental-state score for Ground.
guides.procedure_label: Project-defined self-report scale (mood-1-to-5-v1), not a ground clinical procedure.

sources.title: Mood self-report scale mood-1-to-5-v1
sources.publisher: SYMBIOSIS X project health metrics catalog

guides.title: Symptoms
guides.what: A list of current symptoms, with optional private free text.
guides.why: A structured list makes symptoms comparable over time. The free text adds detail for the crew member only.
how: Select each symptom you notice now from the list.
Add private free text only if it helps; it stays in your onboard private lane.
Record a new entry when symptoms change instead of editing an old one.
guides.context_note: Self-report: symptoms are what the crew member reports, not a diagnosis. Private text stays in the Crew projection and is never sent to Ground.
guides.procedure_label: Project-defined symptom self-report, informed by general patient-reported outcome practice.
